summary: Italian has two ways to say you to one person: tu for people you are close to and Lei for people you keep a polite distance from. The idea that makes it click: Lei is grammatically she, so the verb, the pronouns, the possessive and the imperative all go into the third person singular, and once you have chosen tu or Lei every one of those forms in the sentence must match.

subs.label: who gets tu, who gets Lei
subs.focus: Tu is normal with friends, family, children, fellow students and, in most workplaces, colleagues of the same age; Lei is normal with adult strangers, clients, doctors, officials, shop and hotel staff, and people clearly older than you. These are habits, not laws (many colleagues and neighbours pass to tu quickly), so an item is fair only when the sentence forces the register twice over: a vocative that leaves no doubt (mamma, papà, nonna, Luca said by a friend, ragazzi against signora, signor Bianchi, dottore, professoressa) and, wherever possible, another form already fixed in tu or Lei in the same sentence. A first name alone does not prove tu, and a bare situation in the English cue is weak: put the evidence in the Italian. Typical error of English speakers: tu to everybody because English has one you, or Lei to a child or a close friend. Never build an item on a relationship that Italians themselves handle both ways (a colleague, a neighbour, a friend's parent, a teenager addressing a young shop assistant). Write Lei, La, Le and Suo with a capital in this topic so that the polite forms are visible, but never test the capital: lower case is equally correct and must not be a wrong option or a wrong judge sentence.

subs.label: verb: second person for tu, third for Lei
subs.focus: With tu the verb is second person singular, with Lei third person singular, in every tense: puoi / può, hai / ha, sei / è, vuoi / vuole, come stai / come sta, abiti / abita, hai capito / ha capito, eri / era. The subject pronoun is usually left out, so the verb ending alone shows the register: Signora, ha un documento? Typical errors: a tu verb after a polite vocative or after Lei itself (Signora, hai un documento?; Lei sei molto gentile), and a second person plural taken from English you (Signora, avete un documento?). Offer the voi form as a distractor only rarely and never as the single error of a judge item: voi to one person survives in southern regional use, so the clean contrast is second against third person singular. The English cue must say you, because come sta? alone can also mean how is he or she. Reflexive verbs change the pronoun together with the verb (come ti chiami / come si chiama, ti ricordi / si ricorda): keep both in the same option. Keep the politeness conditional (potrebbe, vorrebbe) out of the answer; it belongs to future-and-conditional.

subs.label: object pronouns: ti against La and Le
subs.focus: Tu has one object pronoun, ti, for direct and indirect objects (ti ringrazio, ti telefono). Lei has two: La for a direct object, used for a man as well as for a woman (La ringrazio, signor Rossi; La chiamo domani; La aspetto qui; La aiuto io; La accompagno), and Le for an indirect object (Le telefono domani, Le scrivo, Le mando una mail, Le dico la verità, Le piace?, Le dispiace aspettare?, Le serve aiuto?). After a preposition the forms are te and Lei (per te / per Lei, con te / con Lei, e tu? / e Lei?). Attached to an infinitive they are written as one word: posso aiutarti / posso aiutarLa, arrivederLa. Typical errors: ti in a Lei sentence, lo for a man addressed politely (lo ringrazio, signor Rossi, meaning you), gli for a man where Le is needed, and La and Le exchanged. Use only verbs whose construction is beyond doubt: ringraziare, chiamare, aiutare, aspettare, accompagnare, salutare, disturbare for La; telefonare, scrivere, dire, mandare, piacere, dispiacere, servire for Le. Avoid verbs that take either pronoun with a different meaning, such as pagare. Never offer arrivederci as wrong in a Lei sentence: it is correct in both registers, and arrivederLa is only the more formal choice. Do not put La before a compound tense (L'ho vista ieri, dottore): usage of the participle ending varies there, so it must not be what an item decides. Write La in full before a vowel (La aspetto). Pairs such as te lo / Glielo belong to combined-pronouns.

subs.label: possessive: tuo against Suo
subs.focus: Your is tuo, tua, tuoi, tue with tu and Suo, Sua, Suoi, Sue with Lei; the ending follows the thing owned, never the sex of the person addressed: il Suo passaporto, la Sua firma, i Suoi documenti, le Sue valigie, and with one unmodified family member no article: Suo marito, Sua moglie, tuo fratello. Typical errors: tuo in a Lei sentence (Signora, ecco il tuo resto), Suo in a tu sentence, Sua because the person addressed is a woman (Signora, il Sua biglietto), and vostro for one person on the model of English your. Vostro is correct when a company or a family is addressed as a group (il vostro ordine), so use it as a distractor only where one private person is clearly meant, and not as the single error of a judge item. The English cue must say your, since suo also means his or her; the sentence needs a polite vocative or a Lei verb so that Suo cannot be read as a third person. The article rules themselves belong to possessives: keep the article correct in every option.

subs.label: imperative: scusa / scusi, senti / senta
subs.focus: The Lei imperative is the third person of the present subjunctive, which looks like the tu ending turned round: verbs in -are have -a for tu and -i for Lei (scusa / scusi, guarda / guardi, aspetta / aspetti, entra / entri), verbs in -ere and -ire have -i for tu and -a for Lei (prendi / prenda, senti / senta, apri / apra, finisci / finisca). Common irregular Lei forms: venga, vada, faccia, dica, dia, stia, abbia, sia, tenga. Pronouns are attached to the tu form and stand before the Lei form: dimmi / mi dica, siediti / si sieda, accomodati / si accomodi, prendilo / lo prenda. The negative is non + infinitive for tu (non ti preoccupare or non preoccuparti, both correct) and non + the same Lei form (non si preoccupi, non aspetti). Typical errors: the tu form to a person addressed with Lei (Scusa, signora; Dimmi, dottore), the Lei form with the pronoun attached (dicami, accomodisi), and the indicative for Lei (Signora, prende pure). Test the choice of register and the place of the pronoun, with the tu forms always spelled correctly; how the tu, noi and voi forms are built belongs to imperative. Keep to high-frequency verbs of everyday requests. Do not set non ti preoccupare against non preoccuparti.

subs.label: greetings and titles that go with each
subs.focus: Ciao belongs to tu, both for hello and for goodbye; with Lei the greetings are buongiorno, buonasera, arrivederci and the more formal arrivederLa. The clash runs one way only: ciao with a Lei form or a polite title is wrong (Ciao, signora, come sta?), but buongiorno, buonasera and arrivederci are also normal with tu (Buongiorno, Marco, come stai?), and salve is neutral, so never mark those as wrong in a tu sentence. Thanks and apologies follow the imperative: scusa / scusi, senti / senta. Titles go with Lei as a rule: signora, signore, signor + surname, dottore, dottoressa, professore, professoressa, avvocato, ingegnere. Before a surname signore, dottore, professore and ingegnere lose the final e (signor Rossi, dottor Bianchi, professor Conti), and a title used to address someone has no article (Buongiorno, signora Ferri, not la signora Ferri). Typical errors: ciao to a stranger or with a title, a polite greeting followed by a tu verb, signore Rossi, and the article before the title in address. Signore alone as a vocative is correct (Scusi, signore). Mostly use the title as the cue that fixes the register for another form; a few items may test ciao against buongiorno or signor against signore directly.

subs.label: adjectives and participles agree with the real person
subs.focus: Although Lei is grammatically feminine, an adjective or a participle with essere that describes the person addressed takes the gender of the real person: Lei è stato molto gentile, dottore; Lei è stata molto gentile, signora; Signor Neri, è sicuro?; Signora, è pronta?; È arrivato ieri, professore? Typical errors: the masculine for a woman because it feels like the neutral form (Signora, è stato molto gentile), and a plural ending (Signora, siete stata, è stati). The sentence must name the person with a title or a first name that shows the sex beyond doubt. Prefer as the wrong form the masculine for a woman or a plural ending; do not use the feminine for a man (Signor Neri, Lei è stata) as the single error of a judge item, because very formal older usage allowed it. Use adjectives with four endings (contento, sicuro, pronto, stanco, occupato, nato) or participles of verbs with essere (arrivato, stato, venuto, andato, rimasto); adjectives in -e show nothing, though gentile is welcome in the sentence outside the tested slot. No participle after the object pronoun La.

subs.label: more than one person: voi in both registers
subs.focus: When you speak to two or more people the form is voi, whether you would say tu or Lei to each of them: Ragazzi, cosa prendete?; Signori, cosa prendete?; Signore e signori, accomodatevi. Everything follows voi: the verb (avete, potete, siete), the pronoun vi (vi ringrazio, vi telefono), the possessive vostro, the imperative (scusate, sentite, accomodatevi, non vi preoccupate), and plural adjectives (siete pronti?). Typical errors: a singular Lei or tu form to several people (Signori, cosa prende?; Ragazzi, hai capito?), ti or La for vi, tuo or Suo for vostro. The sentence must show the plural with a vocative (ragazzi, bambini, signori, a pair of names such as Anna e Paolo, a couple such as signori Rossi). The very formal plural Loro (i signori desiderano?) is still heard in a few hotels and restaurants: never present it as wrong and never use it as the answer or as a distractor.

subs.label: the whole sentence in one register
subs.focus: A sentence with several forms of address must keep all of them in the same register: Scusi, può ripetere il Suo nome? against Scusa, puoi ripetere il tuo nome? This sub-point is the home of rewrite items and of mixed-register judge items. Rewrite: give a tu sentence with two or three dependent forms (imperative or verb, pronoun, possessive, sometimes the greeting and the vocative) and ask for the Lei version, or the reverse; the task names the new listener (Say it to an older stranger., Say it to your friend Luca.), and the tiles must be cut so that each changed form is its own tile and none of the source forms can be reused by accident. Judge: a wrong sentence carries exactly one slip against an otherwise consistent sentence that has at least two other markers of the register (Scusi, puoi ripetere?; Signora, Le porto il tuo caffè; Senti, Marco, mi può aiutare?); a correct sentence is fully in one register. Typical error: starting politely with a fixed formula (scusi, buongiorno, signora) and then sliding into the tu forms that were learned first. Do not count as a slip anything this guide calls correct in both registers: buongiorno or arrivederci with tu, lower-case lei, a first name with Lei. Keep one listener per sentence.

rules.rule: Say tu to friends, family, children and people of your own circle; say Lei to adults you do not know, to clients, doctors, officials and people clearly older than you. When in doubt with an adult stranger, start with Lei.
rules.pattern: mamma, Luca, ragazzo → tu | signora, signor Bianchi, dottore → Lei

examples.tl: Luca, vieni al cinema con noi stasera?
examples.en: Luca, are you coming to the cinema with us tonight?

examples.tl: Signora, viene spesso in questo negozio?
examples.en: Madam, do you often come to this shop?

examples.tl: Mamma, hai visto le mie chiavi?
examples.en: Mum, have you seen my keys?

examples.tl: Dottore, ha un momento per me?
examples.en: Doctor, do you have a moment for me?

rules.note: Italians talk about this choice with dare del tu and dare del Lei. The usual way to pass to tu is to ask: possiamo darci del tu? Lei, La, Le and Suo are often written with a capital in polite writing; lower case is also correct.

rules.rule: Lei takes the verb in the third person singular, the form you use for he or she. Tu takes the second person singular.
rules.pattern: tu: puoi, hai, sei, stai, vuoi | Lei: può, ha, è, sta, vuole

examples.tl: Ciao Sara, come stai?
examples.en: Hi Sara, how are you?

examples.tl: Buongiorno, signor Rossi, come sta?
examples.en: Good morning, Mr Rossi, how are you?

examples.tl: Scusi, può ripetere, per favore?
examples.en: Excuse me, can you repeat that, please?

examples.tl: Signora, Lei è di Milano?
examples.en: Madam, are you from Milan?

rules.note: The word Lei is usually left out, like tu: the verb ending is enough. With a reflexive verb the pronoun changes too: come ti chiami? / come si chiama?

rules.rule: The object pronoun for tu is ti. For Lei it is La when the verb takes a direct object and Le when the verb takes a + person. La is used for a man too.
rules.pattern: ti ringrazio → La ringrazio | ti telefono → Le telefono | per te → per Lei

examples.tl: La ringrazio molto, signor Rossi.
examples.en: Thank you very much, Mr Rossi.

examples.tl: Dottoressa, Le telefono domani mattina.
examples.en: Doctor, I will phone you tomorrow morning.

examples.tl: Signora, Le piace questo colore?
examples.en: Madam, do you like this colour?

examples.tl: Marta, ti chiamo dopo cena.
examples.en: Marta, I will call you after dinner.

rules.note: Attached to an infinitive the pronoun is one word with it: posso aiutarti?, posso aiutarLa? ArrivederLa is the formal goodbye; arrivederci is right in both registers.

rules.rule: Your is tuo with tu and Suo with Lei. The ending agrees with the thing owned, not with the person you are talking to.
rules.pattern: il tuo → il Suo | la tua → la Sua | i tuoi → i Suoi | le tue → le Sue

examples.tl: Signora, questo è il Suo ombrello?
examples.en: Madam, is this your umbrella?

examples.tl: Signor Bianchi, ecco la Sua chiave.
examples.en: Mr Bianchi, here is your key.

examples.tl: Paolo, dov'è la tua macchina?
examples.en: Paolo, where is your car?

examples.tl: Professore, come sta Sua moglie?
examples.en: Professor, how is your wife?

rules.note: Suo also means his or her. The situation, a title or a Lei verb tells you that it means your.

rules.rule: For the Lei imperative swap the vowel of the tu form: verbs in -are take -i (scusi, guardi, aspetti), verbs in -ere and -ire take -a (prenda, senta, apra).
rules.pattern: scusa → scusi | aspetta → aspetti | prendi → prenda | senti → senta | vieni → venga

examples.tl: Scusa, Giulia, sai che ore sono?
examples.en: Excuse me, Giulia, do you know what time it is?

examples.tl: Scusi, signora, sa che ore sono?
examples.en: Excuse me, madam, do you know what time it is?

examples.tl: Prenda pure una sedia, dottore.
examples.en: Do take a chair, doctor.

examples.tl: Aspetti un momento, per favore.
examples.en: Wait a moment, please.

rules.note: Some common Lei forms are irregular: venga, vada, faccia, dica, dia, stia, abbia, sia, tenga.

rules.rule: With the tu imperative the pronoun is attached to the end; with the Lei imperative it stands in front. In the negative, tu has non + infinitive and Lei keeps its own form.
rules.pattern: dimmi → mi dica | siediti → si sieda | accomodati → si accomodi | non ti preoccupare → non si preoccupi

examples.tl: Mi dica, signora, che cosa desidera?
examples.en: Tell me, madam, what would you like?

examples.tl: Dimmi, Andrea, che cosa vuoi?
examples.en: Tell me, Andrea, what do you want?

examples.tl: Prego, si accomodi, il dottore arriva subito.
examples.en: Please take a seat, the doctor is coming right away.

examples.tl: Non si preoccupi, signor Conti, c'è tempo.
examples.en: Do not worry, Mr Conti, there is time.

rules.note: For tu both non ti preoccupare and non preoccuparti are correct.

rules.rule: Ciao goes with tu only. With Lei say buongiorno, buonasera and arrivederci, which are also fine with tu.
rules.pattern: ciao + tu | buongiorno, buonasera, arrivederci + tu or Lei | arrivederLa + Lei

examples.tl: Ciao Matteo, come va?
examples.en: Hi Matteo, how is it going?

examples.tl: Buonasera, signora, desidera un tavolo?
examples.en: Good evening, madam, would you like a table?

examples.tl: Arrivederci, dottore, e grazie di tutto.
examples.en: Goodbye, doctor, and thank you for everything.

rules.note: Salve is a neutral hello, useful when you are not sure which register to use.

rules.rule: Titles normally go with Lei. Before a surname signore, dottore and professore drop the final e, and a title used to address someone has no article.
rules.pattern: signore → signor Rossi | dottore → dottor Bianchi | professore → professor Conti | signora Ferri

examples.tl: Buongiorno, signor Rossi, come sta oggi?
examples.en: Good morning, Mr Rossi, how are you today?

examples.tl: Dottor Bianchi, può venire un momento?
examples.en: Doctor Bianchi, can you come here for a moment?

examples.tl: Scusi, signore, questo posto è libero?
examples.en: Excuse me, sir, is this seat free?

rules.note: Feminine titles do not change: signora Ferri, dottoressa Russo, professoressa Greco. Talking about someone, the article comes back: il signor Rossi non c'è.

rules.rule: With Lei, an adjective or a participle after essere agrees with the real person: masculine for a man, feminine for a woman.
rules.pattern: Lei è stato gentile, dottore | Lei è stata gentile, signora

examples.tl: Lei è stato molto gentile, dottore.
examples.en: You have been very kind, doctor.

examples.tl: Signora, è sicura di questo indirizzo?
examples.en: Madam, are you sure about this address?

examples.tl: Signor Neri, è pronto per il colloquio?
examples.en: Mr Neri, are you ready for the interview?

examples.tl: Professoressa, quando è arrivata a Roma?
examples.en: Professor, when did you arrive in Rome?

rules.note: Only the pronoun is feminine in form. The person you are talking to keeps their own gender.

rules.rule: To two or more people say voi, whether they are friends or strangers. Verb, pronoun, possessive and imperative all take the voi form.
rules.pattern: tu or Lei + tu or Lei → voi: avete, vi, vostro, scusate, accomodatevi

examples.tl: Ragazzi, che cosa prendete da bere?
examples.en: Guys, what are you having to drink?

examples.tl: Signori, avete già ordinato?
examples.en: Gentlemen, have you ordered yet?

examples.tl: Prego, signori, accomodatevi qui.
examples.en: Please, ladies and gentlemen, take a seat here.

examples.tl: Signori Rossi, ecco le vostre chiavi.
examples.en: Mr and Mrs Rossi, here are your keys.

rules.note: A very formal plural with Loro exists, mostly in elegant hotels and restaurants. You will hear it, but voi is always right.

rules.rule: Do not mix. If one form in the sentence is tu, they all are; if one is Lei, they all are: the imperative, the verb, the pronoun and the possessive.
rules.pattern: Scusa, puoi ripetere il tuo nome? ↔ Scusi, può ripetere il Suo nome?

examples.tl: Scusi, può ripetere il Suo nome?
examples.en: Excuse me, can you repeat your name?

examples.tl: Scusa, puoi ripetere il tuo nome?
examples.en: Excuse me, can you repeat your name?

examples.tl: Senta, signora, Le posso fare una domanda?
examples.en: Excuse me, madam, may I ask you a question?

examples.tl: Senti, Chiara, ti posso fare una domanda?
examples.en: Listen, Chiara, can I ask you a question?

rules.note: The usual slip is a polite opening learned by heart (scusi, buongiorno) followed by tu forms. Check every verb and every your and you after it.

right.en: Excuse me, can you repeat that, please?

contrasts.why: Scusi is the Lei form, so the verb must be Lei too: third person può. Puoi belongs with scusa.

right.en: Good morning, Mr Rossi, how are you?

contrasts.why: Signor with a surname addresses the man with Lei, and Lei takes the third person: come sta. Come stai is for someone you call tu.

right.en: Thank you very much, Mr Rossi.

contrasts.why: Ti is the pronoun of tu. Ringraziare takes a direct object, so with Lei the pronoun is La, for a man as well as for a woman.

right.en: Doctor, I will phone you tomorrow morning.

contrasts.why: You phone a qualcuno, so the object is indirect. The Lei pronoun for a + person is Le; La is for verbs with a direct object.

contrasts.wrong: Signora, questo è il tuo ombrello?

right.tl: Signora, questo è il Suo ombrello?

contrasts.why: A woman addressed as signora gets Lei, and the possessive of Lei is Suo. Tuo goes with tu.

right.tl: Mi dica, signora, che cosa desidera?
right.en: Tell me, madam, what would you like?

contrasts.why: Dimmi is the tu imperative, but signora and desidera are Lei. The Lei imperative of dire is dica, with the pronoun in front: mi dica.

right.en: Good evening, madam, would you like a table?

contrasts.why: Ciao is used only with people you call tu. With signora and a Lei verb the greeting is buongiorno or buonasera.

contrasts.wrong: Signora, è sicuro di questo indirizzo?

right.tl: Signora, è sicura di questo indirizzo?
right.en: Madam, are you sure about this address?

contrasts.why: The adjective describes the woman you are talking to, so it is feminine: sicura. Lei does not make everyone masculine or neutral.
Lei is for one person. To several people, even strangers, Italian uses voi: avete.

contrasts.wrong: Buongiorno, signore Rossi, come sta oggi?

right.tl: Buongiorno, signor Rossi, come sta oggi?
right.en: Good morning, Mr Rossi, how are you today?

contrasts.why: Before a surname signore loses its final e: signor Rossi. The full form signore is used alone: scusi, signore.

cheat: Friend, family, child: tu. Adult stranger, client, doctor, signora: Lei.
Lei = she form of the verb: può, ha, è, sta. Never Lei + puoi.
You as object: ti → La (direct: La ringrazio) or Le (a + person: Le telefono).
Your: tuo → Suo, agreeing with the thing: la Sua chiave, il Suo nome.
Imperative: swap the vowel, pronoun in front. Scusa → scusi, dimmi → mi dica.
Ciao only with tu. Two or more people: always voi.
One slip spoils it: after scusi, every verb, pronoun and your stays Lei.
